'''''Pittosporum crassifolium'', karo, stiffleaf cheesewood, kaikaro''' or '''kihiki'''<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.sbs.auckland.ac.nz/uoa/science/about/departments/sbs/newzealandplants/maoriuses/medicinal/trees/karo-pittosporum.cfm |title=Karo, kaikaro, tarata, kōhūhū, koihu |work=Maori uses: Medicinal plants, Trees & Shrubs  |publisher=[[University of Auckland]]}}</ref> is a relatively fast-growing large [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] with an erect, fastigiate [[Habit (biology)|growth habit]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Pittosporum crassifolium Banks & Sol. Ex A.Cunn. (Host Plant) |url=https://plant-synz.landcareresearch.co.nz/DetailsForm.aspx?Type=P&Category=Links&RecordId=384&LSID=URN:LSID:landcareresearch.co.nz:Names:A7696F9F-6919-450C-B3EE-6F1A5469BED2 |website=Plant-SyNZ |access-date=16 March 2023}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> It is [[endemic]] to New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q63848025 |title=Eagle's complete trees and shrubs of New Zealand volume one |last=Eagle |first=Audrey |publisher=Te Papa Press |year=2008 |isbn=9780909010089|location=Wellington, NZ|pages=210|language=English}}</ref> 

This species is self-supporting with a simple form that can grow up to 10 m tall. ''Pittosporum crassifolium'' is part of the wider [[Pittosporaceae]] family, which has over 160 species in the [[Southern Hemisphere|southern hemisphere]].<ref name="New Zealand Trees & Shrubs, A Comprehensive Guide to Cultivation and Identification">{{cite book |last1=Metcalf |first1=L.J |title=New Zealand Trees & Shrubs, A Comprehensive Guide to Cultivation and Identification |date=1972 |publisher=Reed Publishing |location=Auckland}}</ref> 

==Description==
The [[Leaf|leaves]] on this species are approximately 5-10x2-3cm and are oval shaped, dark green and leathery with grey [[Tomentum (botany)|tomentum]] (fine hairs) on the undersides of the leaves including the [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] and [[Inflorescence|inflorescences]].<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Dawson |first1=John |title=New Zealand's Native Trees |last2=Lucus |first2=Rob |date=2019 |publisher=Potton & Burton |isbn=978-0-947503-98-7 |edition= |location=Nelson |pages=532–533}}</ref> This tomentum provides protection against coastal winds by preventing salt damage and moisture loss.<ref name=":2">{{cite book |last1=Eadie |first1=Fiona |title=100 Best New Zealand Native Plants for Gardens |date=2004 |publisher=Random House New Zealand |location=Auckland |isbn=1-86962-069-0 |pages=103–104}}</ref>[[File:Pittosporum crassifolium in Hot Water Beach 03.jpg|thumb|alt=alt text|Leaf shape and green capsules of ''Pittosporum crassifolium''|296x296px]]The leaves are [[Simple leaf|simple]] and are [[Alternate leaf|alternately]] arranged and are very dense at the furthest point away from the [[Plant stem|stem]].<ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=Pittosporum crassifolium |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/pittosporum-crassifolium/ |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |access-date=15 March 2023}}</ref> The leaf [[Leaf margin|margins]] are recurved, thick and leathery (hence the name ''crassifolium'' which translates from [[Latin]] to "thick [[leaf]]")<ref name=":1" /> and they often show signs of [[insect]] damage.<ref name="New Zealand Trees & Shrubs, A Comprehensive Guide to Cultivation and Identification" /> The [[Leaf apex|apex]] of the leaf can vary from being [[Obtuse leaf|obtuse]] (blunt and rounded) to [[Acute leaf|acute]] (sharp and tapered) The [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] are the [[Leaf stalk|stalk]] between the leaf and the [[Leaf stem|stem]], and they measure approximately 4-14x1-3mm.<ref name=":1" />

When in ideal growing conditions, karo can grow into small trees (up to 5 metres (16 ft)) with multiple [[Trunk (botany)|trunks]]. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] on karo is dark brown and black and has distinct [[Lenticel|lenticels]] which allow for breathing. Juvenile plants often appear different from the adult form as the branchlets are covered with tomentum until they mature and become darker.<ref name=":1" />

During the spring to early summer, karo produce fragrant burgundy red [[Flower|flowers]] that are around 10cm long with long stalks and are borne in terminal [[Umbel|umbels]] meaning that they grow in clusters, similar to the shape of an umbrella.<ref name=":3">{{cite book |last1=Fisher |first1=Muriel |title=Growing New Zealand Plants, Shrubs & Trees |last2=Forde |first2=Margaret |date=1994 |publisher=Golden Heights |isbn=1-86953-176-0 |location=Auckland |page=264}}</ref> These terminals are also hairy, unlike the flowers which gives this plant extra protection from salt spray.<ref name=":0" /> The flowers of the karo are [[Plant reproductive morphology|unisexual]], meaning each terminal produces between 5-10 male flowers and up to 5 female flowers.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Adams |first1=N.M |last2=Poole |first2=A.L |title=Trees and Shrubs of New Zealand |date=1979 |publisher=P.D. Hasselberg, Government Printer |location=Wellington|page=82|isbn=0-477-01061-X}}</ref> A distinct feature of the karo flowers is the fragrance which “pervades the evening air”.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cave |first1=Yvonne |last2=Paddison |first2=Valda |title=The Gardener's Encyclopedia of New Zealand Native Plants |date=1999 |publisher=Random House New Zealand |location=Auckland |isbn=1-86962-043-7 |page=265}}</ref> The [[Sepal|sepals]] of the flower (the green part below the flower [[bud]]) measure approximately 7-11mm x 1.5-3mm and they have small [[Cilium|cilia]] (hairs) and brown [[tomentose]] along the margin.<ref name=":1" />

After the karo has flowered, it produces green [[Capsule (fruit)|capsules]], that then develop into woody [[seed pods]] with black [[Seed|seeds]] that are sticky and shiny and are protected inside a [[trigonous]] capsule (three angled) which measures approximately 25mm x25mm and is filled with black glutinous matter.<ref name=":3" />

Although [[Endemism|endemic]] to the upper [[North Island]] of [[New Zealand]], this species has now spread both nationally and internationally and is now considered a [[weed]] in areas where it is non-endemic.

The main way of distinguishing ''Pittosporum crassifolium'' from other native New Zealand pittosporums such as ''[[Pittosporum tenuifolium]]'' and ''[[Pittosporum eugenioides]]'' is the distinct grey tomentum on the underside of the leaves which differs from these other species. The leaves of ''Pittosporum crassifolium'' also have less undulation than these other species.

== Range ==
[[File:Pittosporum crassifolium in Hot Water Beach 09.jpg|thumb|alt=alt text|''Pittosporum crassifolium'', [[Coromandel Peninsula]], New Zealand|left|193x193px]]

Karo's original distribution was generally the top half of the [[North Island]], although now it has naturalised throughout New Zealand and overseas in [[Norfolk Island]], [[Hawaii]]<ref name=nzpcn>{{cite web|title=Pittosporum crassifolium |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.asp?ID=1133 |publisher=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |accessdate=28 May 2012}}</ref> and the [[Isles of Scilly]]. This species has been recorded on [[iNaturalist]] in many other countries. The [[Integrated Taxonomic Information System]] has compiled a list of these countries which includes [[South Africa]], [[Portugal]], [[England]] and [[United States|America]].<ref name=":4">{{cite web |title=Pittosporum crassifolium Banks & Sol. Ex A. Cunn |url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=504426#null |website=Integrated Taxonomic Information System |access-date=15 March 2023}}</ref> These areas where it has been found are all [[Coast|coastal]], which has allowed this species to handle the conditions due to the natural [[Adaptation|adaptations]] it has.

Karo is endemic to the north part of the North Island and is found from [[North Cape (New Zealand)|North Cape]] to [[Poverty Bay]] and in the [[Kermadec Islands|Kermadec]] and [[Chatham Islands]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Alan |first1=H.H |title=Flora of New Zealand. Vol.I. Indigenous Tracheophyta: Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Filicopsida, Gymnospermae, Dicotyledones |date=1961 |publisher=Government Printer |location=Wellington}}</ref> This species has naturally spread through bird dispersal throughout New Zealand and is now a reasonably common [[species]] in the [[South Island]], [[Chatham Islands|Chatham]] and [[Stewart Island|Stewart Islands]]. Because this species wasn’t endemic to the South Island it is now considered an urban weed. It has been widely dispersed by [[Exotic pet|exotic]] and [[Native species|indigenous]] birds.<ref name=":1" />

==Habitat==
Karo can be found in a variety of habitats including forest margins, cliff faces, streamside and rocky areas. The tomentum on the leaf undersides allow for this species to thrive in coastal conditions because the fine hairs help reduce salt damage and prevent moisture loss. Because karo are mainly found in coastal areas and near the [[sea]], they have been referred to as the most tolerant species of New Zealand's tree pittosporums of coastal conditions.<ref name=":0" />  

==Ecology==

===Life cycle and phenology===
[[File:Pittosporum crassifolium (foliage & flowers).jpg|thumb|alt=alt text|Foliage and flowers of ''Pittosporum crassifolium'' during the flowering period|left|200x200px]][[File:Fruitseed Pittosporum Crassifolium HW.jpg|thumb|alt=alt text|Seeds inside the split capsule of the ''Pittosporum crassifolium''|200x200px]]The karo produces dark red [[Flower|flowers]] with a fragrant smell from August to October.<ref name=":1" /> Towards the end of the flowering period, this species produces green capsules which develop into [[seedpods]] with black seeds within. In September, when the fruit is ripe, the capsule splits into three or four valves which have an orange colouring on the inside.<ref name=":0" />

These fruits are then consumed by many different species including [[Rat|rats]] and [[Possums in New Zealand|possums]]. The ripe seed is on the shrub for approximately six months and ripens in winter which allows plenty of time for dispersal via birds and other animals. During spring, this species produces pale green leaves with white tomentum, which creates contrast against the old foliage with the dark leaves and red flowers.<ref name="New Zealand Trees & Shrubs, A Comprehensive Guide to Cultivation and Identification" />

===Growth habit===
Karo prefer to be planted in dry and free draining [[soil]]. This species is happy in sun or shade; however, the height of this species will depend on its exposure to sunlight. When planted in shade karo will stretch to try and find light; however, in a full sun position it tends to have a compacted habit.<ref name=":2" /> When in sun, this species can grow up to 3m tall; meaning in a more sheltered environment it can grow up to 6m tall.<ref name=":2" /> Although this species isn’t fussy about the soil type, if a karo is in [[Waterlogging (agriculture)|waterlogged]] soil it can lose its leaves and it will become weakened.<ref name=":2" /> Karo are also frost sensitive whilst juvenile; however, they are able to tolerate frost and snowfalls once mature.<ref name=":1" /> In order for this species to thrive and have optimal plant growth and health, it should be [[Pruning|pruned]] back to the [[leaf node]] at least once a year. <ref name=":2" />

===Predators, parasites and diseases===
[[File:190307 181 SD Botanic Gdn - New Zealand Garden, Pittosporum crassifolium Karo Tree (47290816362).jpg|thumb|alt=alt text|''Pittosporum crassifolium'' planted as a specimen tree in the New Zealand garden at the San Diego Botanic Gardens |218x218px]]

Karo is a tolerant plant that is mainly [[Pest (organism)|pest]] free. It can be susceptible to [[Psyllidae|psyllids]], but this only causes aesthetic damage to the plant.<ref name=":2" /> However, karo does attract many animals and insects that eat the leaves and fruits. The ITIS has found that some of the main predators are; [[Tui bird|tūī]] (''Prosthemadera novaeseelandiae''), [[silvereye]] (''Zosterops lateralis''), [[western honey bee]] (''Apis mellifera''), [[Common brushtail possum in New Zealand|common brushtail possum]] (''Trichosurus vulpecula''), [[Black-tailed bumblebee|black tailed bumblebee]] (''Bombus melanopygus'') and the [[New Zealand bellbird]] (''Anthornis melanura'').<ref name=":4" /> A study has also been conducted into a new [[Parasitism|parasite]] found on ''Pittosporum crassifolium''. This parasite was identified as ''Zeatylenchus pittosporum'' and it was identified on the species due to the distinct yellow and brown discolouration on the leaves of the karo.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=D |last2=Xu |first2=Y.M |last3=Zhao |first3=Z.Q |title=First report of Zeatylenchus pittosporum on Pittosporum crassifolium |journal=  Australasian Plant Disease Notes|date=2017 |volume=12 |issue=10 |article-number=10 |doi=10.1007/s13314-017-0235-8|bibcode=2017AuPDN..12...10L }}</ref>

==Additional information==
Although karo can be considered a pest, this species can be planted as a specimen tree and is also useful planted as a [[hedge]] or as a [[windbreak]].<ref name="New Zealand Trees & Shrubs, A Comprehensive Guide to Cultivation and Identification" />  

Karo are often mistaken for a [[Feijoa sellowiana|feijoa]] when they are juvenile. This is because they have a very similar form when they are first putting out new growth as the plant appears almost completely grey.<ref name=":2" />

''Pittosporum crassifolium'' is considered to be a "weed in cultivation" in [[California]], where this species is being kept under observation to ensure it does not become invasive.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Harris|first1=Graeme|title=Our Native Plant Invaders|journal=The New Zealand Garden Journal|date=June 2002 |volume=5|issue=1|pages=6–8|publisher=Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture}}</ref>

A study in 2021 tested ''Pittosporum crassifolium'' for [[antimicrobial]] potential and it was found that it can be used as a traditional remedy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Liaqat |first1=A |last2=Iftikhar |first2=A |last3=Zahoor |first3=B |last4=Liaqat |first4=F |last5=Khalid |first5=M, A |last6=Liaqat |first6=F |last7=Ali |first7=L |title=Anti-Microbial Potential of two Traditional Medicinal Plants |journal=Annals of Punjab Medical College |date=2021 |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=134–140 |doi=10.29054/APMC/2021.469|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 }}</ref>
